Use your **own unit materials** whenever you can (assessment briefs, rubrics, policy snippets, reading extracts). If you don’t have anything handy, you can use one of these short, safe texts as a starting point for the summarising and prompting activities.

---

## Sample Text 1 – Workshop Overview (from "What to Expect")

> This session is designed for educators with varying levels of AI experience—from those who've never used AI tools to those already experimenting with them. Our goal is **AI literacy through practical, hands-on experience**, not technical expertise.  
>  
> **Part 1: Welcome & Landscape**  
> – Quick energizer and overview of generative AI  
> – No technical jargon—just practical context  
>  
> **Part 2: Automate the Tedious**  
> – **Hands-on Activity:** Use AI to summarize a complex reading  
> – **Goal:** Experience AI as a time-saving assistant  
> – **You'll try:** Basic prompting for summarisation  
>  
> **Part 3: The Art of the Prompt**  
> – Introduction to the CRAFT framework for better prompts  
> – **Hands-on Activity:** Use Microsoft's Prompt Coach tool  
> – **Goal:** Move from basic to strategic prompting  
>  
> **Part 4: Your 5-Step Critique Framework**  
> – Essential quality control for any AI output  
> – **Hands-on Activity:** Apply the framework to previous outputs  
> – **Goal:** Develop critical evaluation skills  
>  
> **Part 5: Assessment Stress-Test / Unlocking the Impossible**  
> – **Hands-on Activity:** Test one of your assessments against AI or use a multi-step workflow to tackle an "impossible" task  
> – **Goal:** Understand how AI might interact with your assignments and designs  
>  
> **Part 6: Secure, Safe & Sustainable AI**  
> – Core tensions: privacy, accuracy, bias, ethics  
> – **Goal:** Understand responsible AI use  
>  
> **Part 7: Wrap-Up & Next Steps**  
> – Personal AI challenge  
> – Q&A and resources

You can use this text to practise:

- Summarising into bullet points or an LMS announcement.  
- Turning the overview into a short student-friendly email or slide outline.  
- Generating quiz questions about the workshop structure.

## Sample Text 2 – Quick Start Guide (from "Quick Start")

> **The 3 Things You Need to Know**  
>  
> 1. **AI is a Tool, Not a Replacement**  
> – AI assists with tasks; it doesn't replace your expertise  
> – Your judgment is more important, not less  
> – Think "assistant," not "autopilot"  
>  
> 2. **AI Makes Mistakes (Often Confidently)**  
> – Can generate plausible but incorrect information  
> – Doesn't understand context like humans do  
> – **Always verify critical information**  
>  
> 3. **Start Small, Stay Practical**  
> – Pick one repetitive task  
> – Test AI assistance  
> – Evaluate results  
> – Adjust and repeat  
>  
> **For educators, this means:**  
> – Tools that can draft content, answer questions, summarise text  
> – Not magic, not conscious—just pattern-matching at scale  
> – Requires human oversight and expertise

You can use this text to practise:

- Summarising into a very short "What is AI?" paragraph for students.  
- Recasting it as a Week‑1 statement about AI use in your unit.  
- Turning it into a small FAQ or checklist.

## Sample Text 3 – Assessment 2030 Summary

> **Assessment 2030 at Curtin** is a strategic response to generative AI and other emerging technologies. Instead of trying to ban AI, the framework encourages us to design assessments that make **student thinking and judgement visible**, so that human skills stay irreplaceable.  
>  
> It outlines a **two-lane approach**:  
> – **Lane 1:** Secure assessments, such as invigilated exams and controlled tasks, where the focus is on verifying individual performance under defined conditions.  
> – **Lane 2:** Authentic, often collaborative tasks that assume access to technology (including AI) and ask students to use tools transparently while demonstrating their own reasoning, problem-solving, and professional judgement.  
>  
> Assessment 2030 also emphasises **human irreplaceability**—designing tasks where AI can support the process, but cannot replace the learner’s contribution. Examples include iterative portfolios, live defences of ideas, real-world projects, and activities where students must explain or critique AI-generated output.  
>  
> The goal is not simply to stop misconduct, but to prepare graduates for a world where AI is part of everyday work, while maintaining academic integrity, inclusivity, and alignment with Curtin’s 2030 strategic plan.

You can use this text to practise:

- Summarising Assessment 2030 for colleagues who missed the session.  
- Turning it into a short LMS announcement explaining how AI is allowed in a specific assessment.  
- Generating 3–5 quiz or discussion questions about AI‑aware assessment design.

---

These sample texts are intentionally generic and safe to copy into AI tools. In the workshop, encourage participants to **swap them out for their own unit materials** whenever that feels more relevant.
